title: Atomic Structure
description: The building blocks of matter — protons, neutrons, electrons, isotopes, ions, electron configuration, and how our understanding of the atom evolved.

notes.heading: Sub-atomic Particles
notes.body: Atoms are composed of three sub-atomic particles: (1) Protons — located in the nucleus, relative charge +1, relative mass 1. The number of protons (atomic number) defines which element an atom is. (2) Neutrons — located in the nucleus, relative charge 0, relative mass 1. Neutrons help stabilise the nucleus by counteracting the repulsion between positively charged protons. (3) Electrons — orbit the nucleus in shells (energy levels), relative charge −1, relative mass approximately 0 (1/1836 of a proton). In a neutral atom, the number of electrons equals the number of protons — the positives and negatives cancel. The nucleus is extremely small compared to the overall atom: if an atom were the size of a football stadium, the nucleus would be about the size of a pea. Most of the atom is empty space.

illustration.alt: Labelled diagram of an atom showing protons, neutrons and electrons in shells around the nucleus.
illustration.caption: The nucleus contains protons and neutrons; electrons occupy energy levels or shells around it.

notes.heading: Atomic Number and Mass Number
notes.body: Every element is defined by its atomic number (Z) — the number of protons in the nucleus. This never changes for a given element. The mass number (A) is the total number of protons + neutrons in the nucleus. Written in nuclide notation: the mass number is written as a superscript before the symbol, the atomic number as a subscript (e.g., ¹²₆C for carbon-12). To find the number of neutrons: neutrons = mass number − atomic number. Example: sodium ²³₁₁Na has 11 protons, 23 − 11 = 12 neutrons, and (in a neutral atom) 11 electrons. The periodic table lists elements by atomic number. The mass number shown on the periodic table is the relative atomic mass — a weighted average of all naturally occurring isotopes (which is why it is rarely a whole number, e.g., chlorine = 35.5).

illustration.alt: Diagram explaining nuclide notation using carbon-12 and how to calculate neutrons from mass and atomic numbers.
illustration.caption: The top number is the mass number (protons + neutrons); the bottom number is the atomic number (protons).

notes.heading: Isotopes and Relative Atomic Mass
notes.body: Isotopes are atoms of the same element (same number of protons) with different numbers of neutrons. They have the same chemical properties (same electron configuration) but different physical properties (different masses). Examples: carbon-12 (¹²C, 6p + 6n), carbon-13 (¹³C, 6p + 7n), carbon-14 (¹⁴C, 6p + 8n — radioactive, used in carbon dating). Chlorine has two main isotopes: ⁷⁵% ³⁵Cl and ²⁵% ³⁷Cl. The relative atomic mass (Aᵣ) is the weighted mean of all isotopes: Aᵣ(Cl) = (75 × 35 + 25 × 37) ÷ 100 = 35.5. This explains why many atomic masses on the periodic table are not whole numbers. Calculating Aᵣ: multiply each isotope's mass by its percentage abundance, sum these products, divide by 100. Note: the relative atomic mass is a ratio comparing the average mass of an atom to 1/12 the mass of a carbon-12 atom — hence 'relative' (no units).

illustration.alt: Diagram showing carbon-12, carbon-13 and carbon-14 isotopes and the relative atomic mass calculation for chlorine.
illustration.caption: Isotopes have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons; relative atomic mass is a weighted average.

notes.heading: Electron Configuration and Shells
notes.body: Electrons occupy shells (energy levels) around the nucleus. The shells fill from the lowest energy level outward: 1st shell — maximum 2 electrons. 2nd shell — maximum 8 electrons. 3rd shell — maximum 8 electrons (in MYP; the full capacity is 18 but we use 8 for GCSE/Y7-9). 4th shell — maximum 2 (for the first 20 elements). Rule: fill the inner shells first before placing electrons in outer shells. Electron configuration is written as a sequence (e.g., sodium = 2,8,1). The group number of an element (for Groups 1, 2, 13-18) is equal to the number of electrons in the outer shell. The period (row) number equals the number of occupied electron shells. Example: magnesium (atomic number 12, Group 2, Period 3) = 2,8,2 — 3 shells, 2 outer electrons. The outer shell electrons determine chemical reactivity and bonding behaviour. Atoms are most stable with a full outer shell (8 electrons — the 'octet rule', or 2 for the first shell). This drives chemical reactions.

illustration.alt: Bohr-model diagram of a sodium atom with electron shells filled 2, 8, 1.
illustration.caption: Sodium's electron configuration is 2,8,1: three occupied shells place it in Period 3 and one outer electron places it in Group 1.

notes.heading: Ions: When Atoms Gain or Lose Electrons
notes.body: An ion is a charged particle formed when an atom gains or loses electrons (protons stay the same). Metals (Groups 1, 2, 3) lose electrons to form positive ions (cations): Na → Na⁺ + e⁻ (sodium loses 1 electron → 2,8,8, full outer shell). Mg → Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻. Non-metals (Groups 15, 16, 17) gain electrons to form negative ions (anions): Cl + e⁻ → Cl⁻ (chlorine gains 1 electron → 2,8,8). O + 2e⁻ → O²⁻. The charge on the ion equals: (number of protons) − (number of electrons). An atom is neutral because protons = electrons. Losing electrons makes it positive; gaining electrons makes it negative. Ions have the electron configuration of the nearest noble gas — this is why Group 1 forms +1 ions (loses 1 electron to become like neon), Group 2 forms +2, Group 17 forms −1 (gains 1 electron), Group 16 forms −2. Common misconception: ions are NOT atoms — atoms are neutral; ions are charged particles (can be single atoms or groups of atoms like SO₄²⁻).

illustration.alt: Diagram showing a sodium atom losing an electron to become Na+ and a chlorine atom gaining an electron to become Cl-.
illustration.caption: Metals lose electrons to form positive cations; non-metals gain electrons to form negative anions.

notes.heading: History of Atomic Models
notes.body: Our understanding of the atom has evolved through experimentation: (1) John Dalton (1803) — 'billiard ball' model: atoms are indivisible, solid spheres; every element has its own type of atom. (2) J.J. Thomson (1897) — discovered the electron; proposed the 'plum pudding' model: negatively charged electrons embedded in a positive sphere. (3) Ernest Rutherford (1911) — Gold foil experiment: fired alpha particles at thin gold foil. Most passed straight through, but a few were deflected strongly — sometimes bouncing back. Conclusion: most of the atom is empty space with a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus. (4) Niels Bohr (1913) — proposed that electrons orbit the nucleus in fixed energy levels (shells), explaining why electrons do not spiral into the nucleus. (5) James Chadwick (1932) — discovered the neutron, explaining the missing mass in the nucleus. (6) Modern quantum model — electrons exist in orbitals (probability clouds), not fixed orbits. For MYP/Y7, the Bohr model (electrons in shells) is sufficient. Key point: scientific models change as new evidence emerges — this is how science works.

illustration.alt: Timeline of atomic models from Dalton through Thomson, Rutherford, Bohr, Chadwick and the modern quantum model.
illustration.caption: Atomic models changed as new experimental evidence emerged, from solid spheres to quantum probability clouds.

notes.heading: Radioactivity (Introduction)
notes.body: Some isotopes are unstable — their nuclei break down spontaneously, emitting radiation. This is radioactivity. Three types of radiation: (1) Alpha (α) — a helium nucleus (2p + 2n), large and heavy, can be stopped by paper or skin, highly ionising. (2) Beta (β) — a fast-moving electron emitted when a neutron turns into a proton, stopped by a few mm of aluminium, moderately ionising. (3) Gamma (γ) — electromagnetic wave (not a particle), highly penetrating, stopped by thick lead or concrete, weakly ionising. Radioactive decay is random — you cannot predict when an individual nucleus will decay, but you can predict the behaviour of large numbers (half-life). Uses: medical imaging and cancer treatment (gamma rays), smoke detectors (alpha — americium-241), carbon dating (beta from ¹⁴C), nuclear power (controlled fission). Risks: ionising radiation can damage DNA and cause mutations/cancer. Safety: limit exposure time, increase distance from source, use shielding. Background radiation comes from rocks (granite — radon gas), cosmic rays from space, and medical procedures.

illustration.alt: Diagram comparing alpha, beta and gamma radiation and the materials that stop each type.
illustration.caption: Alpha is stopped by paper, beta by aluminium and gamma is only reduced by thick lead or concrete.

flashcards.definition: The number of protons in the nucleus of an atom — uniquely identifies the element.
flashcards.example: All carbon atoms have 6 protons; atomic number of carbon = 6.

flashcards.definition: The total number of protons + neutrons in the nucleus of an atom.
flashcards.example: Carbon-12: 6 protons + 6 neutrons = mass number 12. ²³Na: 11 protons + 12 neutrons = mass 23.

flashcards.definition: Atoms of the same element (same number of protons) with different numbers of neutrons. Same chemical properties, different masses.
flashcards.example: ¹²C (6p + 6n), ¹³C (6p + 7n), ¹⁴C (6p + 8n). ¹⁴C is radioactive and used in carbon dating.

flashcards.definition: The weighted mean mass of all naturally occurring isotopes of an element compared to 1/12 the mass of a carbon-12 atom.
flashcards.example: Chlorine Aᵣ = 35.5 because it is 75% ³⁵Cl and 25% ³⁷Cl: (75×35 + 25×37) ÷ 100 = 35.5.

flashcards.definition: The arrangement of electrons in shells around the nucleus. Written as a sequence: 2,8,1 for sodium (atomic number 11).
A charged particle formed when an atom gains or loses electrons. The number of protons remains unchanged.
flashcards.example: Na → Na⁺ + e⁻ (loses 1 electron → +1 ion). Cl + e⁻ → Cl⁻ (gains 1 electron → −1 ion).

flashcards.definition: A positively charged ion, formed when a metal atom loses electrons.
flashcards.example: Ca²⁺ (calcium loses 2 electrons), Al³⁺, K⁺. Cations are smaller than their parent atoms.

flashcards.definition: A negatively charged ion, formed when a non-metal atom gains electrons.
flashcards.example: O²⁻ (oxygen gains 2 electrons), F⁻, S²⁻. Anions are larger than their parent atoms.

flashcards.definition: Atoms tend to gain, lose, or share electrons to achieve a full outer shell of 8 electrons (or 2 for hydrogen and helium) — the electron configuration of a noble gas.
flashcards.example: Sodium (2,8,1) loses 1 electron to become Na⁺ (2,8) — same configuration as neon.

flashcards.definition: Alpha particles fired at thin gold foil; most passed through, a few deflected. Proved the atom is mostly empty space with a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus.
flashcards.example: Rutherford: 'It was as if you fired a 15-inch shell at tissue paper and it came back and hit you.'

flashcards.definition: A helium nucleus (2 protons + 2 neutrons) emitted from an unstable nucleus. Low penetration (stopped by paper/skin), high ionisation.
flashcards.example: Americium-241 in smoke detectors emits alpha particles — smoke particles block the radiation, triggering the alarm.

flashcards.definition: The time taken for half the radioactive nuclei in a sample to decay. Each isotope has a characteristic half-life — from fractions of a second to billions of years.
flashcards.example: Carbon-14 half-life = 5,730 years — used to date organic material up to ~50,000 years old.

questions.stem: An atom has atomic number 8 and mass number 16. How many neutrons does it have?
questions.explanation: Neutrons = mass number − atomic number = 16 − 8 = 8. This is oxygen.

questions.stem: What determines which element an atom belongs to?
questions.explanation: The number of protons (atomic number) is unique to each element. Change the number of protons, and you change the element.

questions.stem: What is the electron configuration of aluminium (atomic number 13)?
questions.explanation: Shell 1 = 2, Shell 2 = 8, Shell 3 = 3. Total = 2 + 8 + 3 = 13 electrons.

questions.stem: Isotopes of the same element have the same number of protons but different numbers of:
questions.explanation: Isotopes have the same atomic number (protons) but different mass numbers due to different numbers of neutrons.

questions.stem: In a neutral atom, which relationship is always true?
questions.explanation: A neutral atom has equal numbers of positive protons and negative electrons, so the overall charge is zero.

questions.stem: Chlorine has two isotopes: 75% ³⁵Cl and 25% ³⁷Cl. What is its relative atomic mass?
questions.explanation: Aᵣ = (75 × 35 + 25 × 37) ÷ 100 = (2625 + 925) ÷ 100 = 35.5. This is why chlorine's atomic mass on the periodic table is not a whole number.

questions.stem: A magnesium ion Mg²⁺ has 12 protons and 10 electrons. What is its overall charge?
questions.explanation: Charge = protons − electrons = 12 − 10 = +2. Magnesium lost 2 electrons to form a +2 cation.

questions.stem: What did Rutherford's gold foil experiment prove about the structure of the atom?
choices: Electrons are embedded in a positive sphere (plum pudding)
The atom is mostly empty space with a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus
Electrons orbit in fixed shells at specific energy levels
questions.explanation: Most alpha particles passed straight through → atom is mostly empty space. A few bounced back → there must be a tiny, dense, positive centre (the nucleus).

questions.stem: Why does sodium (Group 1, 2,8,1) form a +1 ion?
choices: It gains 1 electron to fill its outer shell
It loses 1 electron to achieve the stable electron configuration of neon (2,8)
It gains 7 electrons to fill its outer shell
questions.explanation: Sodium has 1 electron in its outer shell. By losing that electron, it achieves the stable 2,8 configuration of neon — easier than gaining 7 electrons.

questions.stem: Which type of radiation can be stopped by a sheet of paper?
questions.explanation: Alpha particles are large and heavy (helium nuclei). They are the least penetrating — stopped by a few cm of air or a sheet of paper — but the most ionising.

questions.stem: An atom of ³⁹₁₉K (potassium) has how many neutrons?
questions.explanation: Mass number (39) minus atomic number (19) = 20 neutrons. Protons = 19; electrons (neutral atom) = 19.

questions.stem: Which electron configuration represents a noble gas?
questions.explanation: Noble gases (Group 18) have full outer shells — 2,8,8 is argon. Full outer shells make noble gases extremely unreactive.

questions.stem: A chlorine atom gains 1 electron. What ion does it form, and what is its electron configuration?
questions.explanation: Chlorine (2,8,7) gains 1 electron to become Cl⁻ with configuration 2,8,8 — the same as argon. It gains 1 electron, so the charge is −1.

questions.stem: Why is the plum pudding model no longer accepted?
choices: It was disproved by Rutherford's experiment — if the positive charge was spread out, alpha particles would not have been strongly deflected backwards
Scientists decided to change it without evidence
questions.explanation: The plum pudding model predicted that alpha particles would pass through with only slight deflection — like bullets through pudding. Rutherford observed some bouncing back, which required a concentrated positive charge (the nucleus).

questions.stem: The half-life of iodine-131 is 8 days. If you start with 100 g, how much remains after 24 days?
questions.explanation: 24 days ÷ 8 days per half-life = 3 half-lives. After 1: 50 g. After 2: 25 g. After 3: 12.5 g remains.

questions.stem: An atom of ²⁷₁₃Al (aluminium) has how many neutrons?
questions.explanation: Neutrons = mass number − atomic number = 27 − 13 = 14. Protons = 13; electrons (neutral atom) = 13.

questions.stem: Two atoms have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons. Are they atoms of the same element?
choices: Yes — the number of protons alone defines the element
No — different numbers of neutrons means different elements
Only if they also have the same mass number
Only if they have the same number of electrons
questions.explanation: Element identity depends only on the number of protons (atomic number). Atoms with the same protons but different neutrons are isotopes of the same element.

questions.stem: ¹²C and ¹⁴C are isotopes of carbon. What do they have in common?
questions.explanation: Both have 6 protons — that is what makes them carbon. ¹²C has 6 neutrons and ¹⁴C has 8, so their mass numbers and physical properties differ.

questions.stem: A neutral atom of nitrogen has 7 protons. How many electrons does it have?
choices: It depends on the number of neutrons
questions.explanation: In a neutral atom, electrons = protons, so nitrogen has 7 electrons. The 14 option confuses electrons with the mass number (7 protons + 7 neutrons).

questions.stem: Boron has two isotopes: 20% ¹⁰B and 80% ¹¹B. What is its relative atomic mass?
questions.explanation: Aᵣ = (20 × 10 + 80 × 11) ÷ 100 = (200 + 880) ÷ 100 = 10.8. The 10.5 option is the plain average of 10 and 11 — it ignores the abundances.

questions.stem: In Rutherford's gold foil experiment, why did most alpha particles pass straight through the foil?
choices: The atom is mostly empty space
Alpha particles are too small to be deflected
The foil was too thin to contain atoms
questions.explanation: The nucleus is tiny compared to the whole atom, so almost every alpha particle travelled through empty space without going near a nucleus.

questions.stem: Which sequence shows the atomic models in the correct chronological order?
choices: Dalton (solid sphere) → Thomson (plum pudding) → Rutherford (nuclear) → Bohr (electron shells)
Thomson (plum pudding) → Dalton (solid sphere) → Bohr (electron shells) → Rutherford (nuclear)
Dalton (solid sphere) → Rutherford (nuclear) → Thomson (plum pudding) → Bohr (electron shells)
Bohr (electron shells) → Rutherford (nuclear) → Thomson (plum pudding) → Dalton (solid sphere)
questions.explanation: Dalton proposed solid spheres (1803); Thomson's plum pudding followed his discovery of the electron (1897); Rutherford's nuclear model came from the gold foil experiment (1911); Bohr added electron shells (1913).

questions.stem: Which type of radiation is so penetrating that only thick lead or concrete reduces it significantly?
choices: None — all are stopped by paper
questions.explanation: Gamma rays are electromagnetic waves, not particles, so they interact weakly with matter — the most penetrating type. Beta is stopped by a few mm of aluminium; alpha by paper.

questions.stem: The half-life of carbon-14 is about 5,700 years. A sample starts with 80 g of carbon-14. How much remains after 17,100 years?
questions.explanation: 17,100 ÷ 5,700 = 3 half-lives. After 1: 40 g. After 2: 20 g. After 3: 10 g remains. The 26.7 g option wrongly divides by 3 instead of halving three times.
